```{r, include = FALSE}
library(badgers)
```

# Introduction

The BADGERS (Bayesian ADaptive Graph-guided Errors-in-variables Regression
Solution) package provides tools for a graph-guided Bayesian regression model
for high-dimensional data with replicated covariates and measurement error.
The main workflow samples the latent covariates, the regression coefficients,
the measurement error variance and the graph-guided shrinkage parameters
jointly through an MCMC sampler. The working graph couples the
predictor-specific shrinkage parameters through a constrained Wishart prior,
so that connected predictors receive related shrinkage without being forced
to have the same effect.

The package implements:

1. `badgers()`  
  The primary user-facing function. It fits a grid of `(mu, nu)` values, and
  optionally `psi`, and selects the final combination using the validation
  mean squared prediction error (MSPE).

2. `badgers_mcmc()`  
  The fixed-`(mu, nu, psi)` sampler used internally by `badgers()`. This is useful
  for large-scale parallel workflows where each grid point is run separately.

3. `dg()` and `dg_batch()`  
  Simulation utilities that generate data sets with a true or noisy working
  graph.

This vignette outlines the expected data format and the basic model-fitting
interface.

The model has no intercept or automatic preprocessing. It assumes zero-mean
latent covariates; estimate any centering/scaling on training data and apply it
to the held-out sets. Validation and test responses are used only for scoring.
Use validation MSPE for tuning and reserve the test set for final evaluation.

# Simulation Setup

`badgers` expects, for each of the training, validation (tuning) and test
sets, a response vector of length `n` and a three-dimensional array of
replicate measurements with dimension `num_rep` by `n` by `p`. The working
graph is a `p` by `p` 0/1 adjacency matrix.

Predictors may have different numbers of replicates, as when genes are
measured by different numbers of probes. Put the replicates of predictor `j`
in the first rows of `W[, , j]` and pad the remaining rows with `NA`, using
the same pattern for every observation and for all three sets. The inputs are
checked before sampling, and a layout that violates this rule is reported
with an error message.

The following example simulates a setting with `p = 8` predictors in 2
pathways, three replicates per predictor and a sparse response.

```{r simulation-setup}
library(badgers)

seed <- 123

n <- 12
p <- 8
burnin <- 50
n_iter <- 100
```

The simulated data are generated with `dg()`, whose defaults are the settings
of the paper. Setting `Gmode = 0` gives the sampler the true graph;
`Gmode = 1` with `Gthres = 0.75` keeps the 75% of the true edges with the
largest absolute partial correlations and fills the rest with random edges.
The four scenarios of the paper combine `rho2 = 2` or `rho2 = 5` (low or high
measurement noise) with the true or the noisy working graph.

```{r simulate-data}
sim <- dg(
  seed = seed,
  p = p,
  g = 2,
  gsm = 2,
  ntrain = n,
  ntune = n,
  ntest = n,
  sigma2 = 2,
  rho2 = 2,
  num_rep = 3,
  qmin = 2,
  qmax = 3,
  edii = 0.6,
  ediu = 0,
  eduu = 0.3,
  Gmode = 0,
  Gthres = 1
)

beta_true <- sim$beta
```

# Running BADGERS

Use `badgers()` to fit the `(mu, nu)` grid and select the pair with the
smallest validation MSPE. The example below searches over `mu, nu` in
`{1, 3}` with `psi` fixed at its default of 6 and reports the test MSPE and
the selected predictors. To tune `psi` as well, as in the paper, pass for
example `psi_grid = 2:6`.

```{r badgers-fit}
set.seed(456)
fit <- badgers(
  ytrain = sim$y, Wtrain = sim$W,
  ytune = sim$ytune, Wtune = sim$Wtune,
  ytest = sim$ytest, Wtest = sim$Wtest,
  adj_graph = sim$graph,
  mu_grid = c(1, 3),
  nu_grid = c(1, 3),
  n_iter = n_iter,
  burnin = burnin
)

print(fit)

cat("Test MSPE:", fit$best_result$MSPE_test, "\n")
cat("True nonzero coefficients:", which(beta_true != 0), "\n")
cat("Selected by 95% interval:", which(fit$best_result$CI95 != 0), "\n")
cat("Selected by 90% interval:", which(fit$best_result$CI90 != 0), "\n")
cat("Selected by 80% interval:", which(fit$best_result$CI80 != 0), "\n")
```

# Fixed-(mu, nu, psi) MCMC

For a single fixed `(mu, nu, psi)`, call `badgers_mcmc()` directly:

```{r fixed-mu-nu}
set.seed(789)
fit_one <- badgers_mcmc(
  ytrain = sim$y, Wtrain = sim$W,
  ytune = sim$ytune, Wtune = sim$Wtune,
  ytest = sim$ytest, Wtest = sim$Wtest,
  adj_graph = sim$graph,
  mu = 3,
  nu = 3,
  n_iter = n_iter,
  burnin = burnin
)

cat("Tuning MSPE:", fit_one$MSPE_tune, "\n")
cat("Test MSPE:", fit_one$MSPE_test, "\n")
cat("Selected by 95% interval:", which(fit_one$CI95 != 0), "\n")
cat("Selected by 90% interval:", which(fit_one$CI90 != 0), "\n")
cat("Selected by 80% interval:", which(fit_one$CI80 != 0), "\n")
```

The paper settings are `n_iter = 10000` and `burnin = 5000`, which are the
defaults of `badgers()` and `badgers_mcmc()`. This vignette uses 100 and 50
to demonstrate the interface. Run longer independent chains and assess mixing,
effective sample sizes, and sensitivity before inference. Iteration counts
alone do not establish convergence; adaptation continues after burn-in. For large grids, see the `parallel-runs` vignette for a template that
runs fixed-`(mu, nu, psi)` jobs in parallel and combines the MSPE values afterward.

# Selecting Predictors

`CI95`, `CI90` and `CI80` hold the posterior mean of each coefficient, set to
zero when the 95%, 90% or 80% credible interval covers zero. The 80% intervals
are the ones used for gene selection in the data applications of the paper.
A predictor is selected when its entry is nonzero.

```{r credible-interval}
which(fit_one$CI95 != 0)
which(fit_one$CI90 != 0)
which(fit_one$CI80 != 0)
```

Other levels can be computed from the coefficient trace `BETA`, whose columns
are the MCMC iterations:

```{r credible-interval-other}
beta_post <- fit_one$BETA[, (burnin + 1):n_iter, drop = FALSE]
ci70 <- t(apply(beta_post, 1, quantile, probs = c(0.15, 0.85)))
which(ci70[, 1] > 0 | ci70[, 2] < 0)
```

# References

Hu, Z., Qu, K., Long, Q., Yan, J., and Li, W. A Graph-Guided Bayesian
Regression Model for High-Dimensional Data with Replicated Covariates and
Measurement Error. Manuscript.
